extracted.intended_audience: Stanford researchers/inventors (faculty, students, staff) and prospective licensees
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining patentability, preparing a patent application, interacting with counsel, and prosecuting patent applications (targeted to university inventors and technology licensors). Covers document contents, legal standards (novelty, utility, non-obviousness), inventorship, disclosure duties, and prosecution procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject-matter requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is a set of exclusive rights granted for a limited period of time in exchange for a disclosure of an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentable inventions must be new, useful and non-obvious. The patent is intended to publicly disclose the best mode of practicing an invention and to point out features that distinguish the invention from prior art. A patent typically includes drawings and a specification with sections such as field, background, drawing descriptions, disclosure, detailed description, industrial applicability, and at least one claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel (novelty) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To be considered novel, an invention must be the inventor's original work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inventor must file within one year of: publication anywhere in the world; public use in the U.S.; or an offer for sale in the U.S. The U.S. grants a one-year "grace period" after first public disclosure, but most foreign countries have no grace period — any public disclosure before filing can bar foreign patenting. In patent law, "publication" is interpreted broadly (written or oral); contact OTL with questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Useful (utility) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention will be considered useful if it has some qualitative benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patent application must specify a demonstrable utility for the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-obviousness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentable invention must be "non-obvious" to someone of "ordinary skill in the art."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hypothetical person of ordinary skill is not necessarily an expert but someone knowledgeable with access to relevant prior art. Non-obviousness often describes "unexpected results." Examples of non-obviousness: a new combination of old elements producing a new result; prior failed attempts by others; prior art "teaching away" from the invention. Expert affidavits may be required to show non-obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of the invention (application section)
rubrics_metrics.description: The field of the invention briefly describes the general field of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sentence or two is sufficient to aid the Patent Office in assigning the application to an Examiner and classifying the resulting patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background section (prior art and duty to disclose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The background section describes the work done in the past and what has prompted the inventor to pursue this invention; this information is referred to as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventors have an absolute duty to disclose all relevant prior art. The background typically develops the progression of work and sets forth shortcomings of the prior art; inventors should include all prior art and describe shortcomings and differences between each prior art reference and the invention. Typical prior art sources include journal articles, conference proceedings, issued patents, and other printed materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings and supporting figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings are provided to aid in understanding the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where drawings do not aid understanding or are impractical they may be omitted, but nearly all inventions will have some drawing. Graphs and tables may also be included. Prepare informal but uncluttered labeled sketches to aid the attorney's draftsman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brief description of the drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: The brief description of the drawings merely identifies the view shown in each figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The summary sets forth in broad terms what the inventor considers to be the invention and what advantages are gained by the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be written broadly and typically paraphrases the broadest claim; it does not include all intricate operational details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed description / enablement and best mode
rubrics_metrics.description: The detailed description sets forth the theory and the intricate details of at least one way (sometimes several ways) the invention can be implemented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This description must be detailed enough for someone skilled in the art to reconstruct the invention and must include a description of the best way, in the inventor's view, the invention can be implemented. Each implementation is an "embodiment"; the best one is the "preferred embodiment." Include multiple embodiments and alternative implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims (scope and drafting tradeoffs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims circumscribe the legal bounds of the invention and are generally written using specialized terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should describe essential elements, first broadly and then more narrowly. Narrow claims are easier to obtain but may be easier to design around. To determine if a product falls within a claim, compare the product to each element of the claim — all elements must be present. Patent prosecution centers on debate over claim breadth/narrowness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims determine inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent application claims determine who is and who is not an inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims define the invention from a legal viewpoint and thus guide inventorship determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor is a person who conceives of an original and non-obvious idea which can be described clearly — the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person who contributed a basic idea that resulted in development of the claimed invention is an inventor. A person who contributed only labor or routine supervision but not to the inventive concept is not an inventor (e.g., a technician simply translating an idea into a physical embodiment). Extraneous ideas that do not contribute directly to the claimed invention do not make someone an inventor. Joint inventors have joint rights. Do not confuse inventorship with scientific authorship — criteria differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing for the attorney interview (materials checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before meeting the attorney, collect and briefly summarize all relevant printed materials, publications and/or patents and prepare supporting materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare rough sketches, graphs, and/or tables with labels; list many alternative implementations, improvements, and uses; prepare a description of the preferred embodiment; prepare a description of advantages and uses; prepare a glossary of terms. These materials aid the attorney and draftsman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney interview conduct (how to present)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance for interacting with the patent attorney during the interview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't assume the attorney knows the subject matter in detail. Develop the theory behind your invention from a very basic level. Don't skip steps in derivations. Explain all possible embodiments and applications. Have your files and pertinent materials easily accessible and, if practical, show the physical embodiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-interview review and assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: After the attorney prepares a draft application you will receive a copy to review and provide comments, and later sign formal documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out any errors or misrepresentations and explain changes since the interview. After the final draft, you will be asked to sign an oath/declaration stating you are the inventor and sign an assignment of the application to the Board of Trustees of The Leland Stanford Junior University. Treat your copy of the application, filing date, and serial number as confidential and keep them secure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution timing, responses, and amendment options
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent prosecution is an iterative process with the PTO often issuing rejections that must be answered within set timeframes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An Examiner will usually reject all or some claims in a first Office Action. The attorney will ask you to comment and may need additional information. There is a three-month response window to the Examiner (extendable month-by-month for three months by paying extra fees). The attorney may prepare amendments to modify claim scope or argue against the Examiner. If rejections become final, options include filing a divisional application, a continuation-in-part (CIP), a continuation, or appealing to the PTO Board of Appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs and licensing input in prosecution decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost of prosecution and likelihood of getting commercially useful claims influence prosecutorial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OTL considers cost and commercial usefulness when determining prosecution strategy; if licensed, the licensee typically has input into whether and how to pursue patenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term and foreign filing timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent prosecution can take many years; a U.S. patent is presumed valid and enforceable for 20 years from the earliest filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-U.S. patent terms vary and are usually effective as of the filing date. If patentable, non-U.S. applications are generally filed within one year after the U.S. filing date to preserve foreign rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: When not to patent / licensing alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all Stanford inventions are patented even if they are licensed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: biological materials where the cell line is controlled by the researcher often need not be patented — a license agreement can forbid transfer and require return or destruction upon termination. Software under copyright is another type of non-patented technology that OTL licenses.
